extracted.intended_audience: government lawyers, claims examiners, military and Treasury/War Department officials, and claimants/counsel handling claims against the United States
extracted.subtask_description: Legal/practical standards and precedents for presenting, evaluating, and paying claims against the United States arising from contracts, torts, salvage, property occupation, target practice, and related military/government activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: No officer authority to settle unliquidated contract claims by supplemental contract
rubrics_metrics.description: No executive or accounting officer has authority to settle by supplemental contract unliquidated claims arising from a breach of contract; resort must be had to the courts for their liquidation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited cases: Cramp & Sons v. U.S., XVII Comp. Dec. 806, 810. Practical effect: claims for unliquidated contractual damages cannot be liquidated administratively by supplemental agreements; parties must seek judicial remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: General rule: no payment of unliquidated damages absent contract/appropriation
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims for unliquidated damages (e.g., crops/fences damaged by troops, property taken by soldiers, damage from target practice, collision with government vessels) are not payable by the Government unless there is an express or implied contract to pay or a Congressional appropriation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numerous Comptroller/Claims decisions deny such claims (examples listed: C. 668; C. 1553; C. 2611; C. 4315; C. 4658; etc.). Exception: where an act of Congress appropriates money for 'leases of land and damages of property' it may include unliquidated damages (C. 16525, May 19, 1904).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lease provisions may validly provide for board-assessed damages for maneuvers
rubrics_metrics.description: It is proper to provide in a lease of land for maneuver purposes that a board will consider and award for damage done to fences, crops, and the like by troops, notwithstanding such claims are unliquidated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an explicit exception to the rule against paying unliquidated damages when the lease contemplates such a procedure (C. 16525, May 19, 1904). Such provisions are now incorporated in leases for maneuver/target ranges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interest not payable absent express contractual or statutory authorization
rubrics_metrics.description: Except where payment of interest is expressly stipulated by contract or specifically authorized by an act of Congress, the United States is not bound to pay interest on claims prior to rendition of judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorities cited: multiple Comptroller opinions and the act of Mar. 3, 1911 reenacting 'No interest shall be allowed ... unless upon a contract expressly stipulating for the payment of interest.' Practical guidance: do not expect interest payments unless contract/statute allows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Military officers should not stipulate for interest absent statutory authority
rubrics_metrics.description: In the absence of statutory authority, a military officer entering into a contract on behalf of the United States should not agree that delayed payments will carry interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a preventive/procedural rule for contracting officers: avoid inserting interest clauses unless authorized by law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government not legally liable for torts/criminal acts of officers/agents (general rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: The United States is not legally responsible for the torts or criminal acts of its officers or agents, whether by commission or omission; wrongs by such persons are their personal wrongdoing, not the Government's, absent express agreement or statutory provision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited authorities include Angerica v. Bayard, U.S. v. McKee, Judge Story on agency; numerous claims denied for injuries caused by soldiers, thefts, negligent acts, collisions with government vehicles, etc. Practical effect: claims based on torts of government agents are routinely denied administratively and often must be pursued through Congress for appropriations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possible narrow exception for marine torts and Congressional appropriation practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the general rule is nonliability, an exception has been recognized in some opinions for marine torts; even so, claims for marine torts are often not enforceable against the United States and are customarily referred to Congress for appropriation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Comptroller noted doubt about authorization to liquidate marine torts and that practice has been to refer such claims to Congress. Cite: XIII Comp. Dec. 349 and historical practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government agents remain personally liable for torts; claimant may sue the individual
rubrics_metrics.description: While the Government is not liable, the individual officer or agent who committed the tort is personally responsible and may be sued; separate remedies and disciplinary proceedings (e.g., under articles of war) are available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases listed: Little v. Barreme; Cammeyer v. Newton; Osborn v. U.S.; Board of Liquidation v. McComb; Belknap v. Schild. Practical note: claimants may obtain judgment against individuals, and Congress has in exceptional cases appropriated relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive officers cannot contractually assume Government liability for agents' torts without Congress
rubrics_metrics.description: No executive officer is authorized, in the absence of Congressional legislation, to enter into a contract making the United States responsible for tortious or criminal acts of its agents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited cases: C. 14971, Jan. 29, 1904; C. 17585, Feb. 27, 1905. Practical effect: claims asserting contractual assumption of such liability will be rejected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Occupation of private property by troops does not imply obligation to reimburse for accidental destruction
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the Government occupies private property (e.g., in Philippine insurrection) under an implied lease and premises are burned while in their possession, the Government is not liable for destruction absent a finding of negligence or an express/implied obligation to reimburse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: C. 15541, Dec. 2, 1903; C. 25460, Aug. 24, 1909. Practical guidance: occupation alone does not create a compensable duty to repair or reimburse for accidental loss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims arising from lawful Government action (performed lawfully and without negligence) are not compensable
rubrics_metrics.description: If governmental acts (e.g., destruction of a vessel in violation of landing warnings, removal of driftwood, enforcement actions) were legal and non-negligent, the Government will not be responsible for resulting losses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: destruction of boats, seizure or destruction done in obedience to orders (C. 9762); removal of lumber/driftwood which then becomes Government property (G. 20582). Distinguish between legal actions and negligent or unlawful acts which may implicate other remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional authorization for public works can preclude nuisance/damage claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Where Congress authorizes the erection of public works (e.g., coast artillery battery), that declaration of necessity prevents treating the work as a legal nuisance, and the United States will not be liable for consequential damages to adjoining property owners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited: C. 15872, Feb. 9, 1904. If establishment could be a nuisance only by tort of an officer, the Government still is not liable absent express legal obligation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seacoast defenses and target practice conducted under regulation—reimbursement doubtful if due care exercised
rubrics_metrics.description: When seacoast defenses are constructed from Congressional appropriations and target practice is conducted in conformity with Secretary of War regulations, and the garrison exercises due care, claims for reimbursement for injurious effects (e.g., damage to passing vessels) are doubtful to succeed before Congress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 16665, Aug. 11, 1904. Practical implication: injuries incidental to executing Congressional will under regulation are less likely to generate compensation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public property in the actual possession of the United States cannot be subjected to admiralty liens absent congressional authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Public property stands like private property regarding salvage/general average, but when property is in the actual possession of the United States it cannot, absent authority from Congress, be the subject of an admiralty lien to enforce salvage/general-average claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited decisions: R. 21, Feb. 16, 1886; other Comptroller decisions. Exception: circumstances permitting enforcement without disturbing possession or where Congress has authorized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government to advance payment of general average/salvage for private property transported at Government expense
rubrics_metrics.description: Where private property of officers is transported at Government expense and becomes subject to salvage or a general average contribution, the Government should pay such contribution initially and leave reimbursement adjustments between the officers and the United States for later resolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 17725, Mar. 31, 1905. Practical guidance: claimants should expect the Government to step in first, then settle reimbursement internally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shipment mode and liability for general average: officers bear contribution absent contrary stipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: The Government is not required by law or regulation to ship an officer's private property by rail rather than by sea; shipment method should be economical. If sea shipment results in a general-average contribution, the officer (not the Government) should bear the contribution absent an express stipulation otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 20919, Jan. 16, 1907. Practical note: contracting/transport decisions should consider risk of contributions and allocate responsibility by express agreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Salvage entitlement where troops render services beyond official duty
rubrics_metrics.description: If troops save property by exerting themselves beyond requirements of their official duty, they may be entitled to salvage; funds recovered as salvage may be distributed among company funds with appropriate acquiescence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: G. 12721, June 13, 1902. Practical implication: distinguish ordinary official actions (no salvage) from extraordinary salvage services (possible entitlement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Drift/wrecked lumber on military reservations becomes United States property and is not subject to salvage payments to local keepers
rubrics_metrics.description: Lumber, driftwood, and logs cast ashore within military reservations (including portions used for life-saving stations) become property of the United States and should be cared for or disposed of under statutory rules; services performed by life-saving station keepers do not necessarily entitle them to salvage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: G. 20582, Nov. 5, 1906; G. 20721, Dec. 6, 1906. Practical action: dispose of such material per R.S. 1241 if unsuitable for service.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lease provisions for maneuver damages do not cover thefts/larcenies by troops
rubrics_metrics.description: A lease provision that provides for consideration by a board of damage done by troops to fences and crops does not include losses resulting from thefts, larcenies, or other predatory acts committed by troops; the United States is not responsible for such torts absent Congressional authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 16525, May 19, 1904; C. 17585, Feb. 27, 1905. Practical effect: theft/larceny losses remain uncompensated unless Congress acts.
